blocks.content: Picture this. Your phone buzzes at 3 a.m. You are half asleep, squinting at a laptop screen, and you land on a dashboard. Forty graphs. CPU here, memory there, some queue depth panel you do not even remember adding six months ago. Nothing tells you where to look first.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396527425-422442897.png
blocks.alt: A 3am page leading a half asleep engineer to a dashboard and a runbook

blocks.content: That is the exact gap dashboards and runbooks exist to close. A good dashboard should tell you, in about ten seconds, whether the service is healthy or not. A good runbook should tell you exactly what to do next, written days or weeks earlier by someone who was calm and not staring at a pager at 3 a.m.
A good dashboard answers is this healthy. A good runbook answers what do I do now. Neither one is optional once something you built is running in production.

This is the part of observability that barely ever comes up in interviews, and it is exactly the part that separates a team that resolves an incident in ten minutes from a team that is still guessing an hour in. Detecting a problem is only half the job. The other half is making sure a tired human can act on it fast.
1. Introduction

Every team eventually collects metrics, logs, and traces. Far fewer teams put in the work to turn that raw signal into something a stressed, half asleep person can use in the middle of the night. Dashboards and runbooks are that missing layer. They are not glamorous, they rarely show up in a system design diagram, but they are what actually gets used during an incident.

Think of it this way. Your monitoring stack can detect that error rate spiked. That detection is worthless if the person holding the pager cannot quickly tell which service is affected, has to hunt through forty unrelated graphs to find the right one, and then has to improvise a fix from memory while customers are watching a broken checkout page. Dashboards and runbooks are what turns detection into a fast, calm response.
2. What a good dashboard actually shows
blocks.text: 2. What a good dashboard actually shows

blocks.content: A dashboard is not a museum for every metric you have ever collected. It exists to answer one question fast: is this service healthy right now. Everything past that is extra detail you only need once you already suspect something is wrong.
2.1 RED and USE at a glance
blocks.text: 2.1 RED and USE at a glance

blocks.content: Two small frameworks cover most of what a first glance needs. For request driven services, RED works well: Rate, how many requests are coming in, Errors, how many of them are failing, and Duration, how long they are taking. For the underlying resources a service runs on, USE works well: Utilization, how busy the resource is, Saturation, how much work is queued up waiting, and Errors, how often that resource is failing outright.

["RED, for a service: request rate, error rate, and latency (usually p50, p95, p99).","USE, for a resource: utilization, saturation, and error count, applied to CPU, memory, disk, connection pools, and similar."]
items: RED, for a service: request rate, error rate, and latency (usually p50, p95, p99).
USE, for a resource: utilization, saturation, and error count, applied to CPU, memory, disk, connection pools, and similar.

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396527425-167511711.png
blocks.alt: A wall of 40 unrelated graphs next to a clean dashboard with a few RED and USE panels

blocks.title: Fewer panels, not more
blocks.content: A dashboard with six well chosen panels beats one with sixty. If a panel does not help someone decide healthy or not healthy in the first few seconds, it belongs on a deeper dashboard, not the top level one.
2.2 The ten second test

Here is a simple bar to hold every dashboard to. Put it in front of an on call engineer who has never seen this exact dashboard before. Can they tell, within about ten seconds, whether the service is healthy? If the answer is no, the dashboard needs fewer panels, better labels, or a clearer layout, not more data.

["Top row: request rate, error rate, and latency, the three numbers that answer is this service okay right now.","Second row: the resources that most often cause trouble for this specific service, like database connections or queue depth.","Everything else, further down or on a separate deep dive dashboard."]
items: Top row: request rate, error rate, and latency, the three numbers that answer is this service okay right now.
Second row: the resources that most often cause trouble for this specific service, like database connections or queue depth.
Everything else, further down or on a separate deep dive dashboard.

blocks.title: Order the panels by importance, top to bottom
blocks.content: People read dashboards the way they read a page: top left first. Put the panel that answers the most important question in the top left corner, not buried after ten graphs nobody asked for.
3. Overview dashboards versus service specific deep dives
blocks.text: 3. Overview dashboards versus service specific deep dives

blocks.content: Not every dashboard should try to do the same job. It helps to think of dashboards in two tiers: one wide and shallow, one narrow and deep.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396527425-703133219.png
blocks.alt: An overview dashboard flagging one unhealthy service, linking into that service deep dive dashboard

blocks.content: 3.1 Overview dashboard

An overview dashboard shows system wide health at a glance, usually one row per service or one tile per service, with just enough signal to tell you which one is unhealthy. Its job is not depth, its job is pointing you in the right direction fast when you do not yet know where the problem is.
3.2 Service specific deep dive dashboard

A deep dive dashboard exists for exactly one service, and it goes deep on that service internals: per endpoint latency, database connection pool usage, cache hit rate, garbage collection pauses, queue consumer lag, whatever is specific to how that service actually works. You do not open this dashboard first. You open it once the overview dashboard has already told you where to look.

blocks.title: Link the two together directly
blocks.content: The overview dashboard should link straight into each service deep dive dashboard. If someone has to manually search for the right dashboard by name while an incident is active, you have already lost a minute or two you did not need to lose.
4. Common dashboard mistakes
Most dashboards do not fail because nobody built them. They fail because nobody maintained them, and a few very common mistakes creep in over time.

["Too many panels. A dashboard that tries to show everything ends up showing nothing clearly.","No clear hierarchy. Panels are dropped in the order someone thought of them, not in the order a reader actually needs them.","Graphs without units or context. A line going up means nothing if you cannot tell whether up is good or bad, or what the normal range even looks like.","Dashboards nobody actually looks at. Built once after an incident, never opened again, and forgotten by the time the next incident hits."]
items: Too many panels. A dashboard that tries to show everything ends up showing nothing clearly.
No clear hierarchy. Panels are dropped in the order someone thought of them, not in the order a reader actually needs them.
Graphs without units or context. A line going up means nothing if you cannot tell whether up is good or bad, or what the normal range even looks like.
Dashboards nobody actually looks at. Built once after an incident, never opened again, and forgotten by the time the next incident hits.

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396527426-820015467.png
blocks.alt: A dashboard built after an incident that nobody opens again until the next incident, when the team has forgotten it exists

blocks.content: {"headers":["Curated dashboard","Kitchen sink dashboard"],"rows":[["A handful of panels, ordered by importance","Dozens of panels, added over time with no order"],["Every panel has units, labels, and a normal range","Some panels are unlabeled or hard to read at a glance"],["Reviewed and trimmed after every incident","Never revisited once it is built"],["New team members can read it in a minute","Only the person who built it knows what it means"]]}

blocks.title: Dashboards need an owner
blocks.content: A dashboard with no owner slowly rots. Panels break when a metric gets renamed, thresholds stop making sense as traffic grows, and nobody notices until an incident when it is too late to fix it.
5. What a runbook actually is

A runbook is a written, step by step guide for responding to one specific type of incident or alert. It is written in advance, by someone calm, sitting at their desk, thinking clearly about what usually goes wrong and what usually fixes it. It is not improvised at 3 a.m. by someone who is stressed, half awake, and trying to remember what worked last time.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396527426-529348360.png
blocks.alt: A runbook broken into four ordered steps: check dashboards, check deploys, apply fix, verify and update

blocks.content: Think of it like a pilot preflight checklist. Pilots do not rely on memory and improvisation for critical steps, even ones they have done hundreds of times, because stress and fatigue make people skip things or get the order wrong. A runbook applies the same idea to an incident: write the steps down once, calmly, and just follow them when it matters.

blocks.title: Written in advance, used under pressure
blocks.content: The whole value of a runbook comes from the fact that it was written when nobody was panicking. A runbook someone tries to write for the first time during the incident itself is really just improvisation with extra steps.
6. What makes a runbook actually good
blocks.text: 6. What makes a runbook actually good

blocks.content: Writing any document and calling it a runbook is easy. Writing one that actually gets used correctly during a stressful incident takes a few specific things.
6.1 Linked straight from the alert

The single most important property of a good runbook is that the alert itself links directly to it. When someone gets paged at 3 a.m., they should not have to remember which wiki page covers this alert, or search Slack for the last time this happened. The link should be sitting right there in the alert.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396527426-163183868.png
blocks.alt: An alert with a link embedded directly inside it, leading straight to the relevant runbook page

blocks.content: 6.2 Specific, actionable steps, not vague advice
blocks.text: 6.2 Specific, actionable steps, not vague advice

blocks.content: Compare two runbook steps. One says investigate the issue. The other says run this exact command, check this exact dashboard panel, and if this specific condition is true, roll back using this exact command. Only one of those is actually useful to someone who is stressed and cannot think clearly.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396527426-27009089.png
blocks.alt: A vague instruction to investigate the issue next to a specific instruction to run a named rollback command

blocks.content: ["Vague: investigate the issue and see what is wrong.","Specific: open the checkout deep dive dashboard, check the deploy timeline panel for anything in the last 30 minutes, and if a deploy lines up with the spike, run npm run rollback:checkout."]
items: Vague: investigate the issue and see what is wrong.
Specific: open the checkout deep dive dashboard, check the deploy timeline panel for anything in the last 30 minutes, and if a deploy lines up with the spike, run npm run rollback:checkout.

blocks.title: If you cannot copy paste a step, rewrite it
blocks.content: A good test for any runbook step: could someone unfamiliar with this service copy a command straight out of the runbook and run it, without having to interpret what you meant? If not, it is still too vague.
6.3 Verify the fix and communicate status
blocks.text: 6.3 Verify the fix and communicate status

blocks.content: A runbook that stops at apply the fix is only half finished. It also needs to say exactly how to confirm the fix actually worked, which dashboard panel to watch and what value counts as back to normal, and how to communicate status: where to post an update, and who needs to know the incident is resolved.

blocks.title: Do not let anyone declare victory too early
blocks.content: Without a clear verification step, it is easy for someone to apply a fix, see the error rate drop for thirty seconds, and close the incident, only for it to come right back. Spell out how long to watch and what recovered actually looks like.
7. The alert to runbook relationship

An alert firing and a runbook existing are two separate things, and the gap between them is where most incidents lose their first few minutes. The alert detects the problem. The runbook tells you what to do about it. The relationship only works if the alert points straight at the runbook, every single time it fires.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396527427-930134148.png
blocks.alt: An alert firing, opening its runbook, which points to three dashboards and a rollback command

blocks.content: Paste the runbook link directly into the alert configuration itself, not into a separate document someone has to remember exists. That way it survives regardless of who gets paged, whether it is the person who wrote the runbook or someone who joined the team last week.

blocks.title: A stale runbook is worse than no runbook
blocks.content: If a runbook says run this rollback command and that command no longer exists because the deploy process changed, the responder loses time and trust in every other runbook too. Update the linked runbook as part of every incident postmortem, not as a someday task.
8. Real tooling teams actually use
None of this needs exotic tooling. Most teams reach for the same handful of tools, glued together with a link.

["Grafana, the most common home for dashboards, often backed by Prometheus or a similar metrics store.","Runbooks living as linked wiki pages, Notion or Confluence documents, or a dedicated runbook tool built for incident response.","Some teams skip the wiki entirely for the most common alerts and embed the runbook link directly inside the PagerDuty alert description, so it shows up the moment the page fires."]
items: Grafana, the most common home for dashboards, often backed by Prometheus or a similar metrics store.
Runbooks living as linked wiki pages, Notion or Confluence documents, or a dedicated runbook tool built for incident response.
Some teams skip the wiki entirely for the most common alerts and embed the runbook link directly inside the PagerDuty alert description, so it shows up the moment the page fires.

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396528027-878070239.png
blocks.alt: A PagerDuty alert with a runbook link written directly into its description field

blocks.title: The tool matters far less than the habit
blocks.content: A Notion doc that is actually linked and actually kept current beats a fancy dedicated runbook platform that nobody bothers to update. Pick whatever your team will realistically maintain.
9. Worked example: elevated error rate

blocks.title: Scenario: checkout error rate alert fires at 3 a.m.
blocks.text: Your on call engineer gets paged with an alert titled elevated error rate on checkout service. The alert description includes a direct link to the runbook for this exact alert.

blocks.content: The engineer clicks the link and lands straight on the runbook, no searching required. The runbook says: check these 3 dashboards first, the system overview dashboard, the checkout deep dive dashboard, and the deploy timeline dashboard. Look for any deploy in the last 30 minutes that lines up with when the error rate started climbing.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396528028-567514255.png
blocks.alt: An error rate alert leading to checking the checkout dashboard, spotting a recent deploy, and running the rollback command

blocks.content: The deploy timeline dashboard shows a checkout service deploy went out 12 minutes before the alert fired. That lines up closely enough to be the prime suspect. The runbook next step says: if a recent deploy correlates with the spike, roll it back immediately using npm run rollback:checkout, then confirm the error rate panel on the checkout dashboard returns below 1 percent within 5 minutes.

The engineer runs the rollback command. Four minutes later, the error rate panel drops back to its normal range. Following the runbook last step, they post a short status update in the incident channel: checkout error rate resolved by rolling back deploy from 12 minutes before the alert, monitoring for the next 15 minutes before closing the incident.

blocks.title: Compare this to no runbook at all
blocks.content: Without a linked runbook, the same engineer would have had to remember which dashboards matter for checkout, guess whether a recent deploy was the cause, and recall the exact rollback command from memory at 3 a.m. That is where incidents drag on for an hour instead of resolving in ten minutes.
10. Implementation: a dashboard config and a runbook document
blocks.text: 10. Implementation: a dashboard config and a runbook document

blocks.content: Both a dashboard and a runbook are just documents once you strip away the tooling around them. Here is what each one looks like in practice, kept small enough to actually read during an incident.
10.1 A minimal dashboard panel definition

This is a simplified Grafana style panel definition for the error rate panel that should sit at the very top of the checkout deep dive dashboard. Notice it has a unit, a clear title, and thresholds baked in, so a reader instantly knows whether the number they are looking at is fine or not.

blocks.title: Bake the thresholds into the panel itself
blocks.content: When the color coding lives inside the panel definition, a reader does not have to remember what counts as bad. Green, orange, and red tell the story before they even read the number.
10.2 A real runbook document
This is roughly what the actual runbook for the elevated error rate scenario above looks like, kept short on purpose so it can be read in under a minute while stressed.

# Runbook: Elevated error rate, checkout service

## When this fires
Checkout error rate alert crosses 5 percent for 2 minutes.

## Steps
1. Open the checkout deep dive dashboard: <link>
2. Open the deploy timeline dashboard: <link>
3. Check for any checkout deploy in the last 30 minutes.
4. If a deploy correlates with the spike, run:
   npm run rollback:checkout
5. If no recent deploy, check the payment service dashboard: <link>
   (checkout depends on payment for card charges)

## Verify
Error rate panel on the checkout dashboard back below 1 percent
for 5 straight minutes.

## Communicate
Post an update in #incidents with what was found and what was
done. Keep watching for 15 minutes before closing the incident.

blocks.title: Keep it short, not exhaustive
blocks.content: A ten page runbook does not get read at 3 a.m., it gets skimmed and half followed. A one page runbook with the exact commands you need gets followed completely.
11. The interview angle

It is easy to design a system on a whiteboard and stop at detection: here is my alerting rule, here is my metric. Mentioning dashboards and runbooks on top of that shows an interviewer you have thought past detection, all the way to the human who actually has to respond to the page at 3 a.m.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396528029-509377355.png
blocks.alt: A clear dashboard and a good runbook both feeding into a faster incident resolution

blocks.content: ["Say what your top level dashboard would actually show: RED or USE metrics, not a wall of everything you can measure.","Mention the overview versus deep dive split, and that the overview should link straight into the relevant deep dive.","Bring up runbooks unprompted, and say the alert should link directly to one rather than relying on someone remembering where it lives.","Name a real tool, Grafana for dashboards, a wiki page or PagerDuty description for the runbook link, so it sounds like something you have actually operated, not just read about."]
items: Say what your top level dashboard would actually show: RED or USE metrics, not a wall of everything you can measure.
Mention the overview versus deep dive split, and that the overview should link straight into the relevant deep dive.
Bring up runbooks unprompted, and say the alert should link directly to one rather than relying on someone remembering where it lives.
Name a real tool, Grafana for dashboards, a wiki page or PagerDuty description for the runbook link, so it sounds like something you have actually operated, not just read about.

blocks.content: Good system design candidates do not just design for the happy path or the alert firing. They design for the tired human on the other end of that page, and what that person needs in front of them to fix things fast.
